I covered this earlier in Jan regarding PCB bottlenecks with photonics + $AMZN Kuiper / $SPCX starlink supply chains.

But as an update, it like other industries outside of AI are really starting to feel the pain now too.  

Global Electronics Association: "Is issuing this Industry Alert on escalating shortages across the printed circuit board (PCB) supply chain. 

Companies in automotive, industrial, medical, defense, and telecommunications report longer lead times and difficulty securing supply as AI absorbs scarce capacity, effectively putting production at risk"

The association meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028. The association urged buyers to plan ahead for supply constraints and manufacturers.

Hyperscalers like $AMZN already planned ahead of time taking stakes in Gold Circuit Electronics (2368) for supply procurement... 

But can't say the same about other industries procurement (medical industry is probably not used to competing with hyperscalers over the same supply lol). 

The resulting shortages of critical materials, including CCLs and fibreglass cloth, are squeezing supplies for consumer electronics.

TLDR: same bottleneck, same timeline for 2028. It's just interesting to see association warnings about it impacting medical to defense industries. 

So there's incremental information that it's become an industry wide allocation issue. 

I also think it's helpful to see escalating shortages + broadening... so it might show the selloff is starting to look very disconnected with fundamental demand.
@aleabitoreddit we need more posts and long term outlooks from you in times like these

Thanks, I'll try to make more higher signal fundamental posts. I tend to post more random stuff when I'm stressed (especially with the broader market crash)

But it is pretty wild to see the disconnect between supply procurement patterns and valuations during this deleveraging period.

What you read on Twitter (individual engineers using Claude Code) is very different than what moves the needle for large companies

How to redesign enterprise software development lifecycles, you need to give this a read:

quoted_tweet.author: JD Pruett
quoted_tweet.text:
I've been working with a few orgs with 700+ engineers to redesign their sdlc. they are confused. they've rolled out claude etc., engs are more productive, but they're not seeing almost any of the "speed" startups are feeling right now. i keep telling them, the software part is easy(er). you've got to reorganize people.

read some research today that I think nicely illustrates this. SWE-CoWork (will drop link) found that frontier models completed *less than 8%* of their assignments when they had to track down requirements spread across a 26-person org of AI-simulated colleagues.

Anyone working with an agent day to day can tell you that an agent doing less than 8% of anything is virtually impossible. but also that asking 26 people for requirements is insane (but common).

agent improved when given all requirements up front, but still struggled on changes that touched 60+ files. 

so, some of the speed will be realized when models get better at highly distributed implementations. big labs will do that for you. but the real key to moving faster is redistributing ownership to be narrow and deep, only then followed by said "software factory."

Ruby on Rails creator DHH says AI is bringing back the individual hacker's ability to shape the future of computing:

"I love that we have this energy around computers again, like it was in the '90s, the '80s, where hackers and experimenters are suddenly at the forefront of everything."

"I love this energy that now individuals, thanks to the power of AI, can actually play a pivotal role in the forward progression of the industry."

"Once the internet got sort of bottled up and commercialized, a lot of the frontier work to push things forward just got gobbled up by the big companies."

"We closed off all these domains of the consequential bits of the computer. And only the biggest companies in the world could work on them. And now we're re-democratizing it. We're returning it to the hacker culture. We're returning it to the individual who can actually move some of this stuff forward."

Ruby on Rails creator DHH says the last 2% of building software is where he gets the most satisfaction:

"What we're seeing with a lot of vibecoding projects is they start out and they're kind of promising, and then someone loses interest... Let me just get something done in the first 80%, and then the last 20 is where things are a little janky, they're not quite right, they have some bugs, whatever, and they lose interest."

"For whatever reason, I am blessed with the entire dopamine payoff in the last 2%. I don't actually give a fuck about the first 98. I want the last two. The last two is where I get my satisfaction of building software."

"If you are of that type, that you just keep at it and keep at it and keep at it until it's literally perfect, this is an extremely addictive moment in history because there at least, for the time being, is still a place for someone to drive these agents."

"I've not yet found the correct loop or setup where you can just one-shot everything and the design comes out perfect and everything comes out perfect."

@dhh

DHH says AI could break the app lock-in that has kept new mobile operating systems from competing:

"Microsoft tried. They spent, I don't know, several billion dollars to make Windows OS a thing on mobile, and it wasn't a thing, in huge part because they did not have the applications. Who wanted to switch to a Windows phone if they couldn't get Instagram? So that died on the vine."

"Someone in the Omarchy community rewrote the only application I still kept a Mac around to run, Adobe Lightroom, because it had all my plugins and it had all my presets for my cameras... One guy over the course of, like, two weeks replicated all of Lightroom."

"Now, apply that to a phone, an operating system running on a mobile device that suddenly can get every app you'd ever want, because if it does not exist, someone is gonna come up with it because they can just vibe code it in five minutes."

"The entire lock-in on these ecosystems is about application availability."

@dhh

Nick Bostrom on whether understanding the universe could reveal a shared purpose for humanity:

"If we're in a simulation, then probably the people creating the simulation had some reason for doing that, which is, I guess, depending what you mean by purpose, but there would exist some purpose in that sense."

"One question one might ask... is whether there is some set of facts about the world such that if we understood them clearly, we would basically all come to the same conclusion about what we ought to be doing."

"And if there is such a fact, then maybe you could say that's a kind of objective purpose in some sense."

"If you properly understood all the facts, they would sort of point to the same practical next step. And that, I think, is a lot more of an open question."

Nick joins a16z's Eddy Lazzarin and Elena Burger to discuss what people misunderstand about his views, what “deep utopia” means, and what human purpose might look like in a world with superintelligence.
